title: Gurmukh and manmukh, deeper
hook: he paints the one facing the Guru and the one facing only the self

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true sati: not the one who burns on the pyre, but the one who lives faithfully. Your line was not the pyre.

Which way is your face pointed right now? Not your body. Your attention. Toward the phone, the worry, the next thing you want? Toward someone you love? It's a small question, and Guru Amar Das builds a great deal on it. Near the start of this path we met two words: gurmukh, the one facing the Guru, and manmukh, the one facing only their own mind. In his hymns these aren't labels on a chart. He paints them, like two faces in the same crowded room.
screen: `WHICH WAY ARE YOU FACING?` → `TWO WORDS FROM THE START.` → `HE PAINTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Mukh means face. Gur-mukh, face toward the Guru. Man-mukh, face toward your own mind. Here are some of his strokes, paraphrased from his hymns in Sri Rag and elsewhere. The manmukh is called blind, not because they can't see, but because they see only themselves. They act in ego and call it achievement. They read and recite, yet don't understand. They wander, and the wandering feels like freedom. The gurmukh, in his hymns, is at ease. Speaks sweetly. Sees the One light in everyone. Isn't shaken by praise or blame. Lives in the world with the Name at the center. Now the deeper part. These aren't two kinds of people sorted at birth. They're two directions, and his hymns keep calling the manmukh to turn. The same person can face the Guru at breakfast and only themselves by lunch. That's why his language is so often about turning: the Word turns you around. In the Sikh view, you don't become a gurmukh by deciding you are one. You become one, again and again, by facing the Guru's teaching when the mind would rather face itself. Ego and the Name can't share one room, and which gets it depends on which way the face is turned. So the line today isn't a judgment on anyone. It's a direction.
screen: `MUKH: FACE.` · `BLIND, BECAUSE IT SEES ONLY ITSELF.` · `AT EASE, SEEING THE ONE IN ALL.` · `TWO DIRECTIONS, NOT TWO KINDS.` · then, large: `FACE THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Notice where your attention is facing right now, a worry, a want, a screen, without scolding yourself. Then turn it slowly toward the breath, toward someone you love, or toward a line of the Guru's Word you remember, like man too jot saroop hai, and when it drifts back, turn again: the turning is the practice. If you pray, let Waheguru mark each turn.
Gurmukh and manmukh. The one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind: in Guru Amar Das's hymns, two directions anyone can face. Today's word.
Your line: face the good. Turning again is always allowed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Gurmukh and manmukh run through Guru Amar Das's hymns, which Sikhs hear in kirtan and katha; in Sikh teaching, becoming gurmukh is a lifelong turning toward the Guru's Word.

chat.says: Is a manmukh just a bad person, and a gurmukh a good one?
options: No. They're two directions anyone can face; the same person can turn either way in a day.
Yes. People are born one or the other, and the hymns sort them for good.
No. Gurmukh just means anyone who knows the hymns by heart and recites them.
